title: Mensuration (3D)
summary: Volumes and surface areas of cubes, cuboids, cylinders, cones, spheres, hemispheres, prisms and pyramids, plus melting-recasting, capacities and painted-cube counts. About 1-3 questions per shift; every question reduces to one formula plus a unit conversion, so memorising the formula sheet is nearly the whole job.

subtopics.title: Cube and cuboid
subtopics.concept:
For a cube of edge $a$ and a cuboid $l\times b\times h$:

| Quantity | Cuboid | Cube |
|---|---|---|
| Volume | $lbh$ | $a^3$ |
| Lateral (4 walls) | $2(l+b)h$ | $4a^2$ |
| Total surface | $2(lb+bh+lh)$ | $6a^2$ |
| Space diagonal | $\sqrt{l^2+b^2+h^2}$ | $a\sqrt3$ |

The space diagonal is the **longest rod that fits in the room**. Wall questions use the lateral area only.

tricks.title: Longest rod = space diagonal
tricks.body:
A rod can poke corner-to-corner through the room: $\sqrt{l^2+b^2+h^2}$. Triplets like (3,4,12,13) exist:
$3^2+4^2+12^2=169=13^2$.

example.q: Find the length of the longest rod that can be placed in a room of dimensions $12\text{ m}\times9\text{ m}\times8\text{ m}$.

tricks.title: Painting/flooring picks the right area
tricks.body: Four walls → $2(l+b)h$ (ignore floor and roof). Full painting including roof and floor → TSA. Cost = area × rate.

example.q: A room is 8 m long, 6 m wide and 4 m high. Find the cost of painting its four walls at ₹10 per sq m.

mistakes: Using TSA where the question asks only for the four walls (or the reverse).
Cube diagonal $a\sqrt3$ confused with the face diagonal $a\sqrt2$.
Height left out of the wall formula: walls need $h$; floor area does not.
subtopics.notes:
### The four numbers of a box
For a cuboid of dimensions $l \times b \times h$ (and a cube, where $l = b = h = a$):
| Quantity | Cuboid | Cube |
|---|---|---|
| Volume | $V = lbh$ | $a^3$ |
| Total surface area | $2(lb + bh + lh)$ | $6a^2$ |
| Lateral (4 walls) | $2h(l+b)$ | $4a^2$ |
| Diagonal | $\sqrt{l^2+b^2+h^2}$ | $a\sqrt{3}$ |
| Sum of edges | $4(l+b+h)$ | $12a$ |

These six pairs answer nearly every cube/cuboid question directly. The diagonal formula is the 2-D Pythagoras applied twice — it is the hypotenuse of a right triangle whose legs are a face diagonal and the third edge.

### Units and capacity
Volume in $\text{cm}^3$ converts to millilitres 1:1; $1\ \text{m}^3 = 10^6\ \text{cm}^3 = 1000$ litres. Tank and pit questions: compute $V$ in $\text{m}^3$, multiply by 1000 for litres. Reverse: a "capacity of 50000 litres" tank is $50\ \text{m}^3$. Area-based costs (painting, whitewashing) use the surface area asked — TOTAL for all faces, LATERAL for the four walls of a room (floor and ceiling excluded).

### Composite box work
- Cuboid cut into cubes: number of cubes $= \frac{lbh}{a^3}$ when $a$ divides all dimensions.
- Painting vs carpeting: carpeting is a floor area ($l \times b$); painting four walls is lateral area; painting a closed box is total area. Read which one is priced.
- Sum-of-edges questions: a frame or the total length of edges uses $4(l+b+h)$ — a different quantity from both area and volume.

### Reading the ask, a worked mini-case
"A room 10 m x 6 m x 4 m is to be whitewashed, including the ceiling at Rs 5 per sq m": whitewash covers four walls plus the ceiling (not the floor) $= 2h(l+b) + lb = 128 + 60 = 188$ sq m; cost $= 188 \times 5 = 940$. The same room carpeted is $lb = 60$ sq m; the same room painted fully outside is the TSA. One set of dimensions, four different answers — the exam is testing which surface you price.

### The cube number family
Cubes $1^3$ to $10^3$ (1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216, 343, 512, 729, 1000) and their $6a^2$ (6, 24, 54, 96, 150, 216, 294, 384, 486, 600) cover most reverse questions at sight: TSA 294 → side 7 → diagonal $7\sqrt3$ in two steps. The 3-D diagonal triplets reuse the 2-D ones: edges $(3, 4, 12)$ give diagonal $13$ ($9 + 16 + 144 = 169$), and edges $(2, 3, 6)$ give diagonal $7$ ($4 + 9 + 36 = 49$).

### Quick revision
- $V = lbh = a^3$; TSA $= 2(lb+bh+lh) = 6a^2$; LSA $= 2h(l+b) = 4a^2$.
- Diagonal $\sqrt{l^2+b^2+h^2} = a\sqrt3$; edges $4(l+b+h) = 12a$.
- $1\ \text{m}^3 = 1000$ L; $1\ \text{cm}^3 = 1$ mL.
- Four walls of a room $= 2h(l+b)$; total incl. ceiling $= 2h(l+b) + lb$.

patterns.name: Volume and surface area of cuboid/cube
patterns.howToSpot: Dimensions given; volume or surface area (total/lateral) asked directly.
patterns.logic:
1. Read whether TOTAL (all 6 faces), LATERAL (4 walls) or VOLUME is asked.
2. Substitute; for a cube use the $a$-forms ($a^3$, $6a^2$, $4a^2$).
3. Keep factor form until the last step to avoid arithmetic slips.

Why: each quantity prices a different real thing — capacity, full paint, wall paint — so the ask determines the formula.

example.q: Find the total surface area of a cuboid 12 cm x 10 cm x 8 cm.

patterns.name: Cube specifics: diagonal, lateral area, edges
patterns.howToSpot: A cube's face diagonal/body diagonal, lateral surface, or the total edge length is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Body diagonal: side times $\sqrt3$; face diagonal: side times $\sqrt2$ — do not mix them.
2. Lateral area (4 faces) vs total (6 faces): check the wording.
3. Edge-total questions (frames, wire along edges): $12a$.

Why: the body diagonal spans a face diagonal and the third edge ($a^2 + 2a^2 = 3a^2$), giving the clean $a\sqrt3$.

example.q: The length of the diagonal of a cube of side 6 cm is:

patterns.name: Tank capacity in litres / volume cost
patterns.howToSpot: A tank, pit or room's capacity asked in litres — or digging/painting cost from volume/area at a rate.
patterns.logic:
1. Compute the volume in the stated units; convert BEFORE comparing to rates.
2. $1\ \text{m}^3 = 1000$ L; $1\ \text{cm}^3 = 1$ mL.
3. Cost = (area or volume) x rate — decide which from the wording.

Why: rates are quoted per litre/sq m/cu m, so the conversion is where marks are won or lost.

example.q: A tank is 1.5 m long, 1 m wide and 0.8 m deep. Its capacity in litres is:

patterns.name: Reverse: from volume/area back to a side
patterns.howToSpot: Volume (or surface area) of a cube given — the side, diagonal or edge-sum asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Cube: take the cube root of the volume for the side.
2. From surface area: divide by 6, take the square root.
3. Then answer the actual ask (diagonal $a\sqrt3$, edges $12a$, face area $a^2$).

Why: every cube quantity is a clean power of $a$, so any one of them rebuilds the whole box.

subtopics.title: Cylinder
subtopics.concept:
For a cylinder of radius $r$ and height $h$:
- Volume $=\pi r^2h$ (capacity in litres: multiply $\text{m}^3$ by 1000)
- Curved surface $=2\pi rh$
- Total surface $=2\pi r(r+h)$
- A **hollow pipe/well** of inner radius $r$, outer radius $R$: volume of material $=\pi(R^2-r^2)h$
- A **wire/rod** is a very long thin cylinder: its volume is $\pi r^2\times\text{length}$.

tricks.title: 1 m³ = 1000 litres
tricks.body: Tank answers in litres: compute $\pi r^2h$ in metres, then ×1000. Keep radii in the units the answer needs.

example.q: A cylindrical water tank has a radius of 2 m and a depth of 7 m. Find its capacity in litres. [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]

tricks.title: Hollow cylinder: difference of squared radii
tricks.body: Material volume $=\pi(R^2-r^2)h$ — the cross-section is a ring.

example.q: A metallic pipe has inner radius 3 cm, outer radius 5 cm and length 14 cm. Find the volume of metal. [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]

mistakes: Using the outer radius alone for a hollow pipe.
Forgetting the 1000 factor when the answer is asked in litres.
CSA ($2\pi rh$) and TSA ($2\pi r(r+h)$) mixed up when the question mentions a closed drum or an open tank.
subtopics.notes:
### The three measures
For a cylinder of radius $r$, height $h$:
$$V = \pi r^2 h,\qquad \text{CSA (curved)} = 2\pi r h,\qquad \text{TSA} = 2\pi r(h + r)$$
The curved surface unrolls into a rectangle of width $2\pi r$ (the circumference) and height $h$ — that picture explains every formula. The two circular lids add $\pi r^2$ each for the total.

### Reverse and ratio work
- From volume: $h = \frac{V}{\pi r^2}$; from CSA: $r = \frac{\text{CSA}}{2\pi h}$.
- Changing dimensions: $V \propto r^2 h$, so doubling $r$ quadruples $V$, doubling $h$ doubles it; radius $\times 2$ AND height $\div 2$ leaves $V \times 2$. These multiplier questions are one-line proportion bookkeeping.

### Pipes, wells and flowing water
- **Hollow pipe (tube)**: metal volume $= \pi (R^2 - r^2) \times$ length — the annulus times the length.
- **Well/tank capacity**: compute $V$ in $\text{m}^3$; litres $= 1000 V$.
- **Water flow**: volume delivered per second $= \pi r^2 \times$ (speed); multiply by seconds for the total. Keep the speed units (cm/s) consistent with the radius units.

### Melting and recasting
Melting preserves VOLUME: a cylinder recast into a sphere/wire/spheres keeps $\pi r^2 h$ (with the same metal). Drawn-wire questions: the wire is a thin cylinder of equal volume; if the wire's radius is given as a decimal (0.1 cm etc.), be careful with the fourth power ($r^2$ on both sides).

### The 22/7 number family (with $r = 7$)
- $\pi r^2 = 154$ (base area), $2\pi r = 44$ (circumference).
- CSA $= 44h$: $h = 5 \to 220$, $h = 10 \to 440$, $h = 14 \to 616$.
- $V = 154h$: $h = 10 \to 1540$, $h = 5 \to 770$.
- Radii 14, 21, 3.5 work the same way: $r = 14 \Rightarrow \pi r^2 = 616$; $r = 3.5 \Rightarrow \pi r^2 = 38.5$.
Reverse questions hide in this family: volume 1540 with $r = 7$ is instantly $h = 10$.

### Two worked mini-cases
Pipe: outer R $= 5$, inner r $= 3$, length 14 — ring $= \frac{22}{7}(25 - 9) = \frac{352}{7}$; volume $= \frac{352}{7} \times 14 = 704$ cu cm. The ($R^2 - r^2$) factorises to $(R+r)(R-r) = 8 \times 2$ — sometimes faster.
Flow: a pipe of radius 2 cm delivers water at 10 cm/s for 60 s — volume $= \pi \times 4 \times 10 \times 60 = 2400\pi$ cu cm. Length delivered $=$ speed $\times$ time; the cross-section turns that length into volume.

### Quick revision
- $V = \pi r^2 h$; CSA $= 2\pi rh$; TSA $= 2\pi r(h+r)$.
- $V \propto r^2 h$: radius changes square, height changes linear.
- Pipe metal $= \pi(R^2 - r^2)L$; litres $= 1000 \times \text{m}^3$.
- Melting/recasting: volume is invariant.

patterns.name: Volume / CSA / TSA of a cylinder
patterns.howToSpot: Radius and height given (diameter given — halve it first!); one of volume, curved or total surface asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Identify WHICH measure is asked: capacity → $V$, lateral/curved → CSA, closed drum → TSA.
2. Substitute with $\pi = 22/7$; the memorised (7 → 22, 154, 616) family speeds this up.
3. Keep $\pi$ symbolic until the last multiplication.

Why: the three measures price different real objects (content, label, full metal sheet) — the wording picks the formula.

example.q: Find the volume of a cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm.

patterns.name: Reverse: solve for the missing dimension
patterns.howToSpot: Volume or CSA given with one dimension — the other asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Write the formula; substitute the two knowns.
2. Solve the linear equation for the missing dimension.
3. Sanity-check the size against the given measure.

Why: each formula is linear in $h$ and quadratic in $r$ — solving for $h$ is direct algebra, solving for $r$ means a division then a root.

example.q: The volume of a cylinder is 1540 cu cm and its radius is 7 cm. Its height is:

patterns.name: Hollow pipe and well capacity
patterns.howToSpot: A pipe/tube with outer and inner radii — metal volume; or a well/tank — capacity in litres.
patterns.logic:
1. Pipe: the cross-section is a ring — $\pi(R^2 - r^2)$ — stretched over length $L$.
2. Well: volume $\pi r^2 h$ in $\text{m}^3$, then $\times 1000$ for litres.
3. Watch units: radii in cm with length in m must be matched first.

Why: a hollow solid is the difference of two full solids; a well is just a fat cylinder priced by capacity.

example.q: A cylindrical well has radius 1.4 m and depth 5 m. Its capacity in litres is:

patterns.name: Dimension-change multipliers
patterns.howToSpot: 'Radius doubled, height halved' — by what factor does the volume/surface change?
patterns.logic:
1. Write the volume as $\pi r^2 h$; apply the factor to each symbol.
2. $r \times k$ contributes $k^2$; $h \times m$ contributes $m$.
3. Multiply the contributions; for CSA ($\propto rh$) the factors enter linearly.

Why: radius appears squared in the volume, so its changes compound — the most-tested multiplier fact of the subtopic.

subtopics.title: Cone
subtopics.concept:
For a cone of radius $r$, height $h$ and slant height $\ell=\sqrt{r^2+h^2}$:
- Volume $=\frac13\pi r^2h$ (exactly one-third of the cylinder on the same base)
- Curved surface $=\pi r\ell$
- Total surface $=\pi r(\ell+r)$
- If a cone is rolled from a sector of a circle: the sector's radius is $\ell$, and arc length $=2\pi r$.

The $r$-$h$-$\ell$ triangle is right-angled, so Pythagorean triplets (3,4,5), (7,24,25), (5,12,13) appear constantly.

tricks.title: Triplet for the slant height
tricks.body: Check for (3,4,5) or (7,24,25) among $r,h,\ell$ before computing a square root.

example.q: The radius of a cone is 7 cm and its height 24 cm. Find its curved surface area. [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]

tricks.title: One-third of the cylinder
tricks.body:
Equal base and height: $V_{\text{cone}}=\frac13V_{\text{cylinder}}$ — useful directly in ratio questions and for
conical heaps of sand/grain.

example.q: A conical tent has base radius 7 m and height 24 m. Find its volume. [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]

mistakes: Using $\pi r^2h$ (cylinder volume) for a cone — the one-third is forgotten most often.
Rounding $\ell$ from a non-triplet when exact fractions were expected.
subtopics.notes:
### The cone formulas and the slant triplet
For a right circular cone of radius $r$, height $h$, slant $l$:
$$l = \sqrt{r^2 + h^2},\qquad V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h,\qquad \text{CSA} = \pi r l,\qquad \text{TSA} = \pi r(l + r)$$
The curved surface unrolls into a sector of radius $l$ — that is why $l$ (not $h$) appears in CSA and TSA. Almost every cone question is built on a Pythagorean $(r, h, l)$ triplet, with $(7, 24, 25)$ dominating exams and $(3, 4, 5)$-multiples next. Memorise the whole 7-24-25 family at $\pi = 22/7$:
| given | CSA | TSA | Volume |
|---|---|---|---|
| $r=7, h=24, l=25$ | $550$ | $704$ | $1232$ |

The base circle is always $\pi r^2 = 154$ here, so TSA $= 550 + 154$. A question tripling the size triples nothing — every length scales linearly, areas by $k^2$, volume by $k^3$.

### Reverse routes
- From CSA: $l = \frac{\text{CSA}}{\pi r}$, then $h = \sqrt{l^2 - r^2}$.
- From volume: $h = \frac{3V}{\pi r^2}$ — the factor 3 moving to the top is the classic slip; $r = \sqrt{\frac{3V}{\pi h}}$ likewise.
- Conical heap questions: base circumference first — $r = \frac{C}{2\pi}$ (C $= 44$ m gives $r = 7$ m directly with $\pi = 22/7$).
- Tent questions: canvas $=$ CSA only (no floor). Painted/covered-including-base: add $\pi r^2$.

### Recasting and inscribed relations
Melting preserves volume: a cone recast into a sphere satisfies $\frac{1}{3}\pi r^2 h = \frac{4}{3}\pi R^3$, so $R^3 = \frac{r^2 h}{4}$ — and $r^2 h$ is chosen divisible by 4 in every exam instance. A cone melted into $n$ similar cones divides every length by $\sqrt[3]{n}$ ($n = 27 \Rightarrow$ height $\div 3$).
Solids on the same base with height equal to the radius: $\text{cone} : \text{hemisphere} : \text{cylinder} = \frac13\pi r^3 : \frac23\pi r^3 : \pi r^3 = 1 : 2 : 3$. The largest cone inscribed in a cylinder (same base, same height) holds exactly $\frac13$ of the cylinder.

### Frustum preview
Cutting a cone parallel to its base leaves a frustum: $V = \frac{\pi h}{3}(R^2 + r^2 + Rr)$ — the bucket/tumbler shape, worked in the prism-pyramid subtopic. If instead the TOP piece is asked, it is a smaller similar cone: subtract, or use the similarity ratio directly.

### Quick revision
- $l = \sqrt{r^2+h^2}$; CSA $= \pi r l$; TSA $= \pi r(l + r)$; $V = \frac13 \pi r^2 h$.
- Triplet $(7, 24, 25)$: CSA $550$, TSA $704$, $V$ $1232$, base $154$.
- From $V$: $h = \frac{3V}{\pi r^2}$ (mind the 3). From $C$: $r = \frac{C}{2\pi}$.
- Recast cone → sphere: $R^3 = \frac{r^2 h}{4}$; into $n$ similar cones: lengths $\div \sqrt[3]{n}$.
- Same base & height ($h = r$): cone : hemisphere : cylinder $= 1:2:3$.

patterns.name: Slant height + CSA/TSA with a triplet
patterns.howToSpot: Radius and height given; curved or total surface asked — the $(r, h, l)$ triplet makes $l$ instant.
patterns.logic:
1. Get $l$ from the triplet (7-24-25, 3-4-5 multiples) before any algebra.
2. CSA $= \pi r l$; TSA adds the base: $\pi r(l + r)$.
3. Announce the triplet out loud in the solution — it is the whole speed play.

Why: the curved surface is a sector of radius $l$; the exam numbers are chosen so $l$ is a triplet member.

example.q: The radius of a cone is 7 cm and its height is 24 cm. Its curved surface area is:

patterns.name: Volume of a cone (and reverse)
patterns.howToSpot: Volume asked from $r, h$ — or volume given with a dimension asked (mind the factor 3).
patterns.logic:
1. Third of the cylinder volume with the same base and height.
2. Reverse: $h = \frac{3V}{\pi r^2}$ — bring the 3 up top.
3. Keep $\pi = 22/7$ till the end; thirds cancel cleanly with the 22/7 family.

Why: a cone fills a cylinder of the same base and height exactly one-third — the definition, not just a formula.

example.q: The volume of a cone is 132 cu cm and its base radius is 3 cm. Its height is:

patterns.name: Recasting: cone into sphere/spheres
patterns.howToSpot: A metallic cone melted and recast — the target solid's dimension asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Equate volumes; $\frac{\pi}{3}$ cancels both sides for the cone→sphere case.
2. Solve $R^3 = \frac{r^2 h}{4}$ (or sum the volumes for multiple targets).
3. Take the cube root; the numbers are built to be perfect cubes.

Why: melting is volume-invariant; only the shape of the volume changes.

example.q: A solid metallic cone of radius 6 cm and height 24 cm is melted into a sphere. The radius of the sphere is:

patterns.name: Cone vs cylinder/hemisphere volume ratios
patterns.howToSpot: 'A cone, hemisphere and cylinder stand on the same base and have the same height' — ratio or one volume asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Same base (radius $r$) and height $h = r$: volumes are $\frac13\pi r^3, \frac23\pi r^3, \pi r^3$.
2. Ratio $1 : 2 : 3$; the max cone in a cylinder is $\frac13$ of it.
3. Scale the ratio to the given volume and read off the asked piece.

Why: each volume is a fixed fraction of the cylinder's — the geometry does the dividing for you.

example.q: A cylinder and a cone have equal bases and equal heights. If the cylinder's volume is 120 cu cm, the cone's volume is:

patterns.name: Conical heap / tent (word problems)
patterns.howToSpot: A heap of grain (from base circumference) or a conical tent (canvas = CSA) with real-world wording.
patterns.logic:
1. Heap: circumference → radius → volume $\frac13\pi r^2 h$.
2. Tent: canvas covers the CURVED surface only — $\pi r l$, no base.
3. Compute $l$ via the triplet; watch metre/cm mixing.

Why: a heap has no lid and a tent has no floor — the physical object tells you which formula is 'the surface'.

subtopics.title: Sphere and hemisphere
subtopics.concept:
- Sphere (radius $r$): volume $=\frac43\pi r^3$, surface $=4\pi r^2$.
- Hemisphere: volume $=\frac23\pi r^3$; curved surface $=2\pi r^2$; **total** surface $=3\pi r^2$ (adds the flat circular face).
- Melting and recasting conserves **volume** (surface area almost never matches — that option is a trap).

formulas.name: Hemisphere
formulas.tex: V=\frac23\pi r^3,\quad S_{\text{curved}}=2\pi r^2,\quad S_{\text{total}}=3\pi r^2

tricks.title: Count small balls by the cube of the radius ratio
tricks.body: Number of small spheres $=\left(\frac{R}{r}\right)^3$. Radii in ratio 8:1 → 512 pieces, no π needed.

example.q: A solid metallic sphere of radius 8 cm is melted and drawn into small spheres of radius 1 cm. How many are formed?

tricks.title: Hemisphere TSA is three circles
tricks.body: $3\pi r^2$: two for the curved half (recall the sphere is $4\pi r^2$) plus one for the base.

example.q: Find the total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius 7 cm. [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]

mistakes: Hemisphere TSA taken as $2\pi r^2$ (that is the curved part only).
Melting questions answered with equality of surface areas.
$\frac43\pi r^3$ misremembered as $\frac{4\pi r^3}{3\text{ or }2}$ variants — write the fraction before substituting.
subtopics.notes:
### The sphere family
For a sphere of radius $r$:
$$V = \frac{4}{3}\pi r^3,\qquad \text{SA} = 4\pi r^2$$
For a hemisphere of the same radius: curved surface $= 2\pi r^2$ (half the sphere's), flat face $= \pi r^2$, and total $= 3\pi r^2$ — the famous "3" that examiners love. Volume of a hemisphere $= \frac{2}{3}\pi r^3$.
The radius is the only input: every question is "get $r$, then apply one formula". Given a diameter? Halve it first. Given the surface area? $r = \sqrt{\text{SA}/4\pi}$. Given the volume? $r = \sqrt[3]{\frac{3V}{4\pi}}$.

### Melting, scaling and submersion
- **Melting** preserves volume: a big sphere recast into $n$ small equal spheres gives $r_{\text{small}} = \frac{r}{\sqrt[3]{n}}$ — for $n = 8$ the radius halves, for $n = 27$ it divides by 3.
- **Scaling**: radius $\times k$ → surface $\times k^2$, volume $\times k^3$. "Radius doubled" means SA $\times 4$ and $V \times 8$; "radius halved" gives $\frac14$ and $\frac18$.
- **Submersion**: a solid dropped into a (partly filled) cylinder of base radius $R$ raises the water level by $h = \frac{V_{\text{solid}}}{\pi R^2}$ — the displaced volume spreads over the base.

### Same-base relations
Sphere vs cylinder of radius $r$, height $2r$ (the sphere fits exactly inside): both have volume $\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3$. Sphere vs hemisphere: hemisphere is half the volume, $\frac34$ of the total surface ($3\pi r^2$ vs $4\pi r^2$).

### The 22/7 number family
- $r = 7$: SA $= 616$, $V = \frac{4}{3} \times \frac{22}{7} \times 343 = 4312/3$ — exams avoid it; they use $r = 21$: $r^3 = 9261$, $V = 4 \times 22 \times 441 = 38808$, SA $= 4 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 441 = 5544$.
- Hemisphere at $r = 7$: CSA $308$, TSA $462$; at $r = 21$: CSA $2772$, TSA $4158$.
- The displacement pair worth memorising: a sphere of radius 3 displaces $36\pi$; a cylinder of radius 4 therefore rises $\frac{36}{16} = 2.25$ cm.

### Scaling in percent form
Radius $+10\%$: SA $+21\%$, $V$ $+33.1\%$ (from $1.1^2$ and $1.1^3$). Radius $-50\%$: SA $\frac14$, $V$ $\frac18$ — volume swings harder than area in both directions. Percent-change questions in this subtopic are always these two exponent rules; if you find yourself expanding $\frac{4}{3}\pi$, stop and write $k^2$ or $k^3$ instead.

### Quick revision
- $V = \frac43\pi r^3$; SA $= 4\pi r^2$; hemisphere: CSA $2\pi r^2$, TSA $3\pi r^2$, $V = \frac23\pi r^3$.
- Radius $\times k$: SA $\times k^2$, $V \times k^3$.
- Melt into $n$ equal spheres: radius $\div \sqrt[3]{n}$.
- Water rise: $h = \frac{V_{\text{solid}}}{\pi R^2}$ of the container.

patterns.name: Surface area / volume of a sphere
patterns.howToSpot: Radius (or diameter) given; SA or volume asked — or one of them given and $r$ asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Halve diameters first; then $r$ drives both formulas.
2. With $\pi = 22/7$, the 7-cube of $r = 21$ gives the classic $V = 38808$.
3. Reverse: $r = \sqrt{\text{SA}/4\pi}$ or $r = \sqrt[3]{3V/4\pi}$.

Why: the sphere has a single parameter, so forward and reverse questions differ only by which side you solve for.

example.q: Find the surface area of a sphere of radius 7 cm (take pi = 22/7).

patterns.name: Hemisphere: curved vs total vs volume
patterns.howToSpot: A hemisphere (dome, bowl) — the curved surface, total surface, or volume asked; the TSA = 3*pi*r^2 fact is the trap-setter.
patterns.logic:
1. Dome/tent/scoop of a sphere → hemisphere.
2. Painted outside only → CSA $2\pi r^2$; a solid hemisphere's whole surface → TSA $3\pi r^2$; capacity → $\frac23\pi r^3$.
3. Keep the three straight; the difference is exactly one $\pi r^2$.

Why: half a sphere's skin plus one circular lid — the arithmetic is deliberately easy once the pieces are named.

example.q: Find the total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius 7 cm (take pi = 22/7).

patterns.name: Recasting and water displacement
patterns.howToSpot: A sphere melted into smaller spheres — or dropped into a cylindrical vessel, where the water rise is asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Melting: equate volumes; for $n$ equal spheres divide the radius by $\sqrt[3]{n}$.
2. Displacement: the rise times the container's base area equals the sphere's volume.
3. Watch which radius is which — the sphere's $r$ vs the vessel's $R$.

Why: displaced water is just the volume wearing a different shape; recasting is the same statement in metal.

patterns.name: Radius-scaling multipliers
patterns.howToSpot: 'Radius doubled/halved/increased 50%' — how do surface area and volume change?
patterns.logic:
1. Write the multiplier: $r \to kr$.
2. SA scales $k^2$; volume scales $k^3$ — never the same number.
3. Percent form: radius $+50\%$ → $k = 1.5$ → SA $\times 2.25$, $V \times 3.375$.

Why: area is a product of two lengths, volume of three — the exponents do all the work.

subtopics.title: Prisms, pyramids and painted cubes
subtopics.concept:
- **Prism:** two parallel congruent bases; volume $=$ base area $\times$ height.
- **Pyramid:** volume $=\frac13\times$ base area $\times$ height.
- **Painted cube cut into $n^3$ unit cubes** (side $n$): cubes with 3 painted faces $=8$ (corners);
  2 faces $=12(n-2)$ (edges); 1 face $=6(n-2)^2$; unpainted $=(n-2)^3$.

tricks.title: Painted-cube formula table
tricks.body: Identify $n$ = number of small cubes along one edge. Corners are fixed at 8; the rest depend on $n-2$.

example.q: A cube of side 7 cm is painted on all faces and cut into 1 cm cubes. How many small cubes have exactly two faces painted?

tricks.title: Pyramid by one-third
tricks.body: Same base and height as a prism: the pyramid holds exactly one-third.

example.q: A pyramid stands on a square base of side 10 cm and is 12 cm high. Find its volume.

mistakes: Forgetting the $\frac13$ in pyramid (and cone) volumes.
Painted-cube formulas applied with $n$ = side length in cm instead of cubes per edge.
Counting corner cubes as 6 or edge cubes as $12(n-1)$.
subtopics.notes:
### Prisms and pyramids: the one-third rule
A prism has a constant cross-section: $V = (\text{area of base}) \times (\text{length/height})$. A pyramid with the same base and apex over the centre holds exactly one-third: $V = \frac13 \times \text{base area} \times h$. This is the cone/cylinder relation in flat-base form — the fraction $\frac13$ is the whole topic.
$$V_{\text{prism}} = A_{\text{base}} \times h, \qquad V_{\text{pyramid}} = \frac{1}{3} A_{\text{base}} \times h$$

### Frustums (cut pyramids/cones)
Slice a cone or pyramid parallel to its base and remove the top: what remains is a frustum.
$$V = \frac{\pi h}{3}\left(R^2 + r^2 + Rr\right) \text{ (conical)}, \qquad V = \frac{h}{3}\left(A_1 + A_2 + \sqrt{A_1 A_2}\right) \text{ (any)}$$
with $R, r$ the two radii (or $A_1, A_2$ the two face areas) and $h$ the perpendicular height between them. Bucket and tumbler questions are frustums.

### Lateral surfaces
- Prism lateral area $=$ (perimeter of cross-section) $\times$ (length) — the tube unrolls flat.
- Pyramid lateral area $= \frac12 \times$ (perimeter of base) $\times$ (slant height) — sum of triangles.
The total adds the two base/cross-section ends.

### Cube cutting and melting
A cube of side $a$ cut into unit cubes yields $a^3$ of them. Melting several cubes into one: sum the volumes and take the cube root — edges $3, 4, 5$ combine into a cube of edge $\sqrt[3]{27+64+125} = 6$. Both facts are volume bookkeeping; nothing else changes on melting.

### Worked frustum
Bucket with $R = 5$, $r = 3$, $h = 6$: the bracket $R^2 + r^2 + Rr = 25 + 9 + 15 = 49$, and $\frac{\pi h}{3} = \frac{22}{7} \times 2$, so $V = \frac{22}{7} \times 2 \times 49 = 308$ cu cm. Exam frustums are built so the bracket is a perfect square times $\frac{22}{7}$-friendly numbers — if your bracket is ugly, recheck the radii (diameters halved?) and the terms ($Rr$ included?). For the cut-off top piece instead, either subtract the small cone from the big one or use the similarity ratio: cutting at half the height leaves $\frac18$ of the volume below-cut... rather, the removed top cone has $\frac18$ of the whole cone's volume, so the frustum is $\frac78$ of it.

### Cube numbers worth carrying
$a^3$: 1, 8, 27, 64, 125, 216, 343, 512, 729, 1000, 1331, 1728 — the melting answers live here ($216 \to 6$, $729 \to 9$, $1728 \to 12$). Two cubes of edge $a$ melted give $\sqrt[3]{2a^3} = a\sqrt[3]{2}$ — NOT $2a$; only cube-number sums recast into clean cubes, which is why exams pick $3^3 + 4^3 + 5^3 = 6^3$ (the only consecutive-cube identity).

### Quick revision
- Prism: $V = A \times h$; pyramid: $\frac13 A h$; lateral prism $= P \times h$, pyramid $= \frac12 P l$.
- Frustum (cone form): $\frac{\pi h}{3}(R^2 + r^2 + Rr)$.
- Cut cube of side $a$ into unit cubes: $a^3$ pieces.
- Melted cubes: $\sqrt[3]{\sum a_i^3}$.

patterns.name: Volume of a prism
patterns.howToSpot: A prism/tank/beam with a stated cross-section area (or easy base) and a length — volume or capacity asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Identify the constant cross-section (triangular, rectangular, any).
2. Compute its area, then multiply by the length/height.
3. Capacity questions: $\text{m}^3 \times 1000$ = litres.

Why: a prism is a base 'swept' along a line — the volume is literally area times distance swept.

example.q: A triangular prism has a cross-section area of 20 sq cm and length 12 cm. Its volume is:

patterns.name: Volume of a pyramid
patterns.howToSpot: A pyramid (square/rectangular base) with base side(s) and height given — volume asked, or compared with a prism.
patterns.logic:
1. Base area from the sides; multiply by height.
2. Then take one-third — the step exams test by omitting.
3. Pyramid vs prism of the same base and height: volumes $1 : 3$.

Why: three pyramids fill the matching prism; the one-third is the definition being tested.

example.q: A pyramid stands on a square base of side 10 cm and is 12 cm high. Its volume is:

patterns.name: Frustum of a cone (bucket)
patterns.howToSpot: A bucket/tumbler shape — two radii (or diameters) and the height given; capacity asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Halve diameters to get $R, r$; keep $h$ perpendicular (not slant).
2. Compute $R^2 + r^2 + Rr$; multiply by $\frac{\pi h}{3}$.
3. Litres conversion if the bucket capacity is asked.

Why: a frustum is the big cone minus the small cut-off cone; the three-term formula is its closed form.

example.q: A bucket is in the shape of a frustum with radii 5 cm and 3 cm and height 6 cm. Its volume is (take pi = 22/7):

patterns.name: Cube cutting and melting
patterns.howToSpot: A cube cut into smaller equal cubes — or several cubes melted into one big cube; the count or the new edge asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Cutting: the count is the cube of the side ratio; a cube of side $a$ cm gives $a^3$ unit cubes.
2. Melting: add the volumes, take the cube root — triplet sums like $27+64+125=216$ are favourites.
3. Surface-area questions after cutting: $6N s^2$, larger than the original block.

Why: volume is conserved on cutting/melting; only the shape of that volume is redistributed.

example.q: Three metal cubes of edges 3 cm, 4 cm and 5 cm are melted into a single cube. Its edge is:

patterns.name: Lateral surface of prism / pyramid
patterns.howToSpot: Perimeter of the cross-section (or base) plus a length/slant height — the lateral (side) area asked.
patterns.logic:
1. Prism: the side walls unroll into a rectangle $P \times h$.
2. Pyramid: the sides are triangles — half the base perimeter times the slant height.
3. Add the base area only if TOTAL surface is asked.

Why: both formulas are 'unroll the walls and measure the resulting flat shape'.

example.q: A square pyramid has a base of side 10 cm and slant height 13 cm. Its lateral surface area is:

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Dimensions of a box given; volume, total surface, or the four walls of a room asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: $V = lbh = a^3$; TSA $= 2(lb+bh+lh) = 6a^2$; four walls $= 2h(l+b)$. Read which measure the wording prices.

example.q: Find the total surface area of a cuboid of dimensions $12 \times 10 \times 8$ cm.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A cube's body/face diagonal or the total edge length asked; or volume/area given and the diagonal asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Body diagonal $a\sqrt3$, face diagonal $a\sqrt2$, edges $12a$. Reverse from $V$ or TSA to $a$ first.

example.q: The total surface area of a cube is $294$ sq cm. Find its body diagonal.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Tank/pit capacity in litres, digging cost
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A tank/pit/room's capacity asked in litres, or a cost at Rs x per cu m / per sq m.
pyqPatterns.approach: $1\ \text{m}^3 = 1000$ L; volume for capacity/digging, area for painting. Convert BEFORE applying rates.

example.q: A tank $1.5$ m $\times$ $1$ m $\times$ $0.8$ m holds how many litres?

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Radius and height given (diameter must be halved); volume, curved or total surface asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: $V = \pi r^2 h$, CSA $= 2\pi rh$, TSA $= 2\pi r(h+r)$ with $\pi = 22/7$. Capacity → $V$, label → CSA, closed drum → TSA.

example.q: Find the volume of a cylinder of radius $7$ cm and height $10$ cm.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Cylinder: reverse dimension or multiplier change
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Volume/CSA given with a dimension asked — or 'radius doubled, height halved' style volume changes.
pyqPatterns.approach: $h = \frac{V}{\pi r^2}$, $r = \frac{\text{CSA}}{2\pi h}$; multipliers: $r \times k$ contributes $k^2$, $h \times m$ contributes $m$.

example.q: The radius of a cylinder is doubled and its height halved. Its volume becomes:

pyqPatterns.pattern: Hollow pipe, well capacity, water flow
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A pipe with outer/inner radii (metal volume), a well (litres), or water flowing through a pipe.
pyqPatterns.approach: Pipe metal $= \pi(R^2 - r^2)L$; flow per second $= \pi r^2 \times$ speed; well litres $= 1000 \times \text{m}^3$.

example.q: An iron pipe of length $14$ cm has outer radius $5$ cm and inner radius $3$ cm. Find the volume of iron.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Radius and height given; curved/total surface or volume asked — the $(r, h, l)$ triplet makes $l$ instant.
pyqPatterns.approach: $l = \sqrt{r^2+h^2}$ (7-24-25 family), CSA $= \pi r l$, TSA $= \pi r(l+r)$, $V = \frac13\pi r^2 h$.

example.q: A cone has $r = 7$ cm and $h = 24$ cm. Find its CSA and TSA.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Melted and recast' — a solid's material reshaped; the target dimension asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Equate volumes. Cone→sphere: $R^3 = \frac{r^2 h}{4}$. Into $n$ similar solids: lengths divide by $\sqrt[3]{n}$.

example.q: A metallic cone of radius $6$ cm and height $24$ cm is melted into a sphere. Find the sphere's radius.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A sphere or hemisphere (dome/bowl) with radius given or implied; SA, TSA, or volume asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: $SA = 4\pi r^2$, $V = \frac43 \pi r^3$; hemisphere CSA $2\pi r^2$, TSA $3\pi r^2$, $V \frac23 \pi r^3$. Radius $\times k$: SA $k^2$, V $k^3$.

example.q: Find the volume of a sphere of radius $21$ cm (take $\pi = 22/7$).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: A constant cross-section solid (prism), a pointed solid (pyramid), or a bucket-shaped frustum with volumes asked.
pyqPatterns.approach: Prism $V = A \times h$; pyramid $\frac13 A h$; frustum $\frac{\pi h}{3}(R^2 + r^2 + Rr)$. Cube melts: $\sqrt[3]{\sum a_i^3}$.

example.q: A bucket is a frustum with radii $5$ cm, $3$ cm and height $6$ cm. Find its capacity.

solvedExamples.q: A room is 12 m long, 9 m wide and 8 m high. Find the length of the longest pole that can be placed inside the room.
solvedExamples.solution:
The longest pole fits along the space diagonal:

$\sqrt{12^2+9^2+8^2}=\sqrt{144+81+64}=\sqrt{289}=17$ m.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 12-9-8 → 17 is a stock diagonal: $144+81+64=289=17^2$. Trap: 15 m is the floor diagonal $\sqrt{12^2+9^2}$.

solvedExamples.q: A cylindrical tank of radius 2 m and depth 7 m is full of water. The capacity of the tank is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
solvedExamples.solution:
$V=\pi r^2h=\frac{22}{7}\times4\times7=88$ m$^3$.

$1$ m$^3=1000$ litres, so capacity $=88{,}000$ litres.
solvedExamples.shortcut: $88$ m³ ×1000 → 88,000 L. Trap: 880 (×10) or answering in m³.

solvedExamples.q: A solid metallic cone of radius 6 cm and height 3 cm is melted and recast into a sphere. The radius of the sphere is:
solvedExamples.shortcut: $V_{\text{cone}}=36\pi$; set $\frac43\pi R^3=36\pi$ → $R^3=27$ → 3 cm. Trap: 6 cm (radius unchanged) and 2 cm (took $R^3=36/4$ with a slip).

solvedExamples.q: If each edge of a cube increases by 10%, the percentage increase in its volume is:
solvedExamples.solution:
Volume scales as the cube of the linear factor: $(1.1)^3=1.331$.

Increase $=33.1\%$. (Surface would rise by $(1.1)^2=1.21$, i.e. 21%.)

practice.q: The volume of a cube of edge 6 cm is:
practice.shortcut: $6^3=216$. Trap: 36 is the face area.

practice.q: The total surface area of a cuboid of dimensions $8\text{ cm}\times6\text{ cm}\times4\text{ cm}$ is:
practice.shortcut: Half of 208 is 104 — the bracket sum; double it. Trap: 104 (no doubling).

practice.q: The volume of a cylinder of radius 7 cm and height 10 cm is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.shortcut: $49\times10\times22/7=1540$. Trap: 440 is the CSA ($2\pi rh$).

practice.q: The surface area of a sphere of radius 7 cm is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.shortcut: $4\times154=616$. Trap: 462 is the hemisphere TSA ($3\pi r^2$); 308 is $2\pi r^2$.

practice.q: The total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius 7 cm is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.shortcut: Three circles of $\pi r^2=154$ each → 462. Trap: 308 is only the curved half.

practice.q: The diagonal of a cuboid of dimensions $3\text{ cm}\times4\text{ cm}\times12\text{ cm}$ is:
practice.shortcut: $9+16+144=169=13^2$. This cuboid is a stock triplet (3, 4, 12 → 13).

practice.q: The radius of a cone is 7 cm and its height is 24 cm. Its curved surface area is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.shortcut: 7-24-25 triplet: $\ell=25$, then $\pi\times7\times25=550$. Trap: 528 uses $h$ instead of $\ell$ ($2\pi rh$).

practice.q: A solid metallic sphere of radius 6 cm is melted and drawn into a cylindrical wire of radius 2 mm. The length of the wire is:
practice.solution:
Sphere: $V=\frac43\pi(6)^3=288\pi$ cu cm.

Wire radius: 2 mm $=0.2$ cm. $V_{\text{wire}}=\pi(0.2)^2L=0.04\pi L$.

$0.04\pi L=288\pi\Rightarrow L=7200$ cm $=72$ m.
practice.shortcut: $288\pi/0.04\pi=7200$ cm. Units trap: 2 mm $=0.2$ cm; answer in metres divides by 100. 720 m forgot that step.

practice.q: A metallic pipe has inner radius 3 cm, outer radius 5 cm and length 14 cm. The volume of metal used is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.shortcut: Ring area $22\times16=352$, ×14/2... directly: $\frac{22}{7}\times224=704$. Trap: 1100 uses only the outer cylinder.

practice.q: A solid sphere of radius 8 cm is melted and recast into small spheres of radius 1 cm each. The number of small spheres formed is:
practice.shortcut: Cube the radius ratio: $8^3=512$. Trap: 64 (squared the ratio — that is an area ratio).

practice.q: If each edge of a cube increases by 10%, its volume increases by:
practice.shortcut: $1.1^3=1.331$. Trap: 21% is the surface increase; 30% treats volume as linear.

practice.q: A pyramid stands on a square base of side 10 cm and is 12 cm high. Its volume is:
practice.shortcut: $100\times12=1200$, then one-third → 400. Trap: 1200 forgot the $\frac13$.

practice.q: A hemispherical bowl of internal radius 9 cm is full of water. The water is emptied into a cylindrical bottle of radius 3 cm. The height of water in the bottle is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.shortcut: $486\pi/9\pi=54$. Keep π symbolic — it cancels. Trap: 18 cm uses the bowl volume as $\frac13\pi r^3$.

practice.q: A cube of side 7 cm is painted on all its faces and then cut into 1 cm cubes. How many of the small cubes have exactly two faces painted?
practice.solution: $n=7$: cubes on edges (excluding corners) have exactly two painted faces: $12(n-2)=12\times5=60$.
practice.shortcut: 12 edges × 5 cubes each = 60. Trap: 54 ($6(n-2)^2$ mixing formulas), 75 (5³).

practice.q: A road roller of diameter 84 cm and length 120 cm rolls 500 times over a road. The area of the road levelled is: [Use $\pi=\frac{22}{7}$]
practice.solution:
The roller levels with its curved surface: $CSA=2\pi rh=2\times\frac{22}{7}\times0.42\times1.2=3.168$ sq m.

Area $=500\times3.168=1584$ sq m.
practice.shortcut: CSA in metres ($r=0.42$ m, $h=1.2$ m) is 3.168, then ×500 = 1584. Trap: 3168 doubles it; 792 halves it.

practice.q: The volume of a cuboid of dimensions $8$ cm $\times$ $6$ cm $\times$ $4$ cm is:
practice.shortcut: $lbh = 192$. Trap: adding the dimensions ($18$) or $2(lb+bh+lh)$ when volume is asked.

practice.q: The total surface area of a cuboid of dimensions $12 \times 10 \times 8$ cm is:
practice.shortcut: $2 \times 296 = 592$. Trap: $400$ — that is only $2(lb + bh)$, one face missed.

practice.q: A room is $10$ m long, $6$ m wide and $4$ m high. The area of its four walls is:
practice.shortcut: $2 \times 4 \times (10+6) = 128$. Trap: $240$ (that adds floor + ceiling: $128 + 120$) or $96$ (only $lb \times 2$).

practice.q: The lateral surface area of a cube of side $7$ cm is:
practice.shortcut: Four faces: $196$. Trap: $294$ (six faces) or $343$ (the volume).

practice.q: The sum of the lengths of all edges of a cuboid is $100$ cm and its length, breadth and height are in the ratio $3:2:5$. The length of the cuboid is:
practice.solution:
Edges: $4(l+b+h) = 100 \Rightarrow l+b+h = 25$ cm.

Ratio $3:2:5$ → 10 parts = 25 → 1 part $= 2.5$ cm; length $= 3 \times 2.5 = 7.5$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $l+b+h = 25$; 3 parts of 2.5 = $7.5$ cm. Trap: $10$ cm (the height's 5 parts).

practice.q: The length of the body diagonal of a cube of side $5$ cm is:
practice.shortcut: $5\sqrt3$ (body) vs $5\sqrt2$ (face) — the question says body/longest diagonal.

practice.q: A rectangular tank is $1.5$ m long, $1$ m wide and $0.8$ m deep. Its capacity is:
A pit $10$ m long, $8$ m wide and $2$ m deep is dug. If the cost of digging is Rs $50$ per cu m, the total cost is:
practice.shortcut: Volume first ($160$), then x 50: Rs $8{,}000$. Trap: Rs $1{,}600$ (area x rate).

practice.q: The volume of a cube is $216$ cu cm. Its total surface area is:
practice.shortcut: $a=6$: $6 \times 36 = 216$. (Volume and TSA coincide at $a=6$ — coincidence, not a rule.)

practice.q: The total surface area of a cube is $294$ sq cm. The length of its body diagonal is:
practice.shortcut: TSA → side → diagonal chain: $7\sqrt3$. Trap: $7\sqrt2$ (face diagonal).

practice.q: The volume of a cylinder of radius $7$ cm and height $10$ cm is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $22 \times 7 \times 10 = 1540$. Trap: $770$ (dropped the $r^2$ to $r$).

practice.q: The curved surface area of a cylinder of radius $7$ cm and height $5$ cm is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $44 \times 5 = 220$. Trap: $154$ — that is a $\pi r^2$ piece (one lid).

practice.q: A closed cylindrical drum has radius $7$ cm and height $7$ cm. Its total surface area is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $2\pi r(h+r) = 44 \times 14 = 616$. Trap: $308$ (one lid only).

practice.q: The volume of a cylinder is $1540$ cu cm and the radius of its base is $7$ cm. Its height is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $1540 / 154 = 10$ cm. Trap: $5$ cm (used $2\pi r$ instead of $\pi r^2$).

practice.q: The curved surface area of a cylinder is $352$ sq cm and its height is $8$ cm. Its radius is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $r = \frac{352}{2\pi \times 8} = 7$ cm. Trap: $14$ (forgot the 2 in $2\pi rh$).

practice.q: An iron pipe is $14$ cm long and has an outer radius of $5$ cm and an inner radius of $3$ cm. The volume of iron in the pipe is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: Ring $\times$ length: $22/7 \times 16 \times 14 = 704$. Trap: $1100$ (ignored the hollow core).

practice.q: A cylindrical well has a radius of $1.4$ m and a depth of $5$ m. The water it can hold, in litres, is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $30.8\ \text{m}^3 \times 1000 = 30{,}800$ L. Trap: $3{,}080$ (slipped a factor of 10 in $1.4^2$).

practice.q: The radius of a cylinder is doubled and its height is halved. Its volume becomes:
practice.shortcut: $k^2 m = 4 \times \frac12 = 2$: doubled. Trap: 'unchanged' (the $r^2$ and $h$ effects don't cancel).

practice.q: The radius of a cylinder is increased by $50\%$ and its height is decreased by $20\%$. Its volume changes by about:
practice.shortcut: $1.5^2 \times 0.8 = 1.8$ → $+80\%$. Trap: $+50\%$ (applied $1.5 \times 0.8 = 1.2$, missing a radius power).

practice.q: The radius of a cone is $7$ cm and its height is $24$ cm. Its curved surface area is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $l = 25$ first; $\pi r l = 550$. Trap: using $h=24$ in CSA → $528$.

practice.q: The radius of a cone is $7$ cm and its height is $24$ cm. Its volume is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $\frac{1}{3} \times 22 \times 7 \times 24 = 1232$. Trap: $3696$ (forgot the third).

practice.q: The radius of a cone is $7$ cm and its height is $24$ cm. Its total surface area is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $\pi r(l + r) = 22 \times 32 = 704$. Trap: $550$ (CSA only — the tent answer, not this one).

practice.q: The radius of a cone is $7$ cm and its slant height is $10$ cm. Its curved surface area is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $\pi r l$: $220$. Trap: squaring the slant or using $r^2$.

practice.q: The volume of a cone is $132$ cu cm and its base radius is $3$ cm. Its height is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: Bring the 3 up: $\frac{3 \times 132}{\frac{22}{7} \times 9} = 14$ cm. Trap: $21$ (used $\frac{V}{\pi r^2}$ without the 3).

practice.q: A solid metallic cone of radius $6$ cm and height $24$ cm is melted and recast into a sphere. The radius of the sphere is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $R^3 = \frac{r^2 h}{4} = 216$ → $R = 6$ cm. Trap: $8$ (set $R^3 = r^2 h$ without the 4).

practice.q: A cylinder and a cone have equal base radii and equal heights. If the volume of the cylinder is $120$ cu cm, the volume of the cone is:
practice.solution: Same base and height: cone $= \frac13 \times$ cylinder $= \frac{120}{3} = 40$ cu cm.
practice.shortcut: One-third: $40$. Trap: $60$ (half) — the hemisphere gets that slot.

practice.q: A cone, a hemisphere and a cylinder stand on equal bases and have the same height. If the volume of the cylinder is $300$ cu cm, the volume of the hemisphere is:
practice.solution:
Same base (radius $r$) and height $h = r$: volumes are $\frac13\pi r^3$, $\frac23\pi r^3$, $\pi r^3$ — ratio $1:2:3$ (cone : hemisphere : cylinder).

Cylinder (3 parts) $= 300$ → 1 part $= 100$; hemisphere $= 2 \times 100 = 200$ cu cm.
practice.shortcut: $\frac{2}{3} \times 300 = 200$. Trap: $100$ (that is the cone's share) or $150$ (splitting $300$ in half).

practice.q: The radius of the base of a cone is $5$ cm and its height is $21$ cm. Its volume is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: The 21 and the 7 cancel: $\frac13 \times 21 = 7$. Trap: $770$ (dropped the third).

practice.q: A large metallic cone of height $18$ cm is melted and recast into $27$ small solid cones, each similar in shape to the original. The height of each small cone is:
practice.solution:
Equal shapes: volume ratio $27 = 3^3$ → linear ratio $\sqrt[3]{27} = 3$.

Height $= \frac{18}{3} = 6$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $\sqrt[3]{27} = 3$, so every length divides by 3: $6$ cm. Trap: $2$ cm (dividing by 9, a square root).

practice.q: A heap of wheat is in the shape of a cone. Its base circumference is $44$ m and its height is $3$ m. The volume of the heap is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: Circumference → $r = 7$; then a third: $154$. Trap: $462$ (full cylinder volume).

practice.q: A conical tent has a base radius of $7$ m and a slant height of $25$ m. If canvas costs Rs $2$ per sq m, the cost of the canvas needed to make the tent is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.solution:
Canvas covers the curved surface only: CSA $= \pi r l = \frac{22}{7} \times 7 \times 25 = 550$ sq m.

Cost $= 550 \times 2 = 1100$.
practice.shortcut: CSA $550 \times$ Rs $2$ = Rs $1{,}100$. Trap: Rs $1{,}232$ — that is the volume number, a different measure.

practice.q: The surface area of a sphere of radius $7$ cm is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $4 \times 22 \times 7 = 616$. Trap: $308$ (half — the hemisphere CSA) or $462$ (hemisphere TSA).

practice.q: The volume of a sphere of radius $21$ cm is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
The curved surface area of a hemisphere of radius $7$ cm is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: Half the sphere: $308$. Trap: $462$ — that adds the flat circular face.

practice.q: The total surface area of a solid hemisphere of radius $7$ cm is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: Curved $308$ + flat face $154$ = $462$. Trap: $308$ (forgetting the lid) or $770$ (wrong $4\pi r^2 + \pi r^2$).

practice.q: A solid metal sphere of radius $6$ cm is melted and drawn into $8$ equal small spheres. The radius of each small sphere is:
practice.solution:
$8 = 2^3$ equal spheres → each length divides by $\sqrt[3]{8} = 2$.

Radius $= \frac{6}{2} = 3$ cm.
practice.shortcut: $r = 6/\sqrt[3]{8} = 3$ cm. Trap: $2$ cm (dividing the radius by 3, the wrong root).

practice.q: A solid sphere of radius $3$ cm is dropped into a cylindrical vessel of base radius $4$ cm containing water. The height by which the water rises is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $h = \frac{V}{\pi R^2} = \frac{36}{16} = 2.25$ cm. Trap: $3$ cm (confusing the sphere's radius with the rise).

practice.q: If the radius of a sphere is doubled, its surface area becomes:
practice.shortcut: $k^2 = 4$. Trap: $8$ times — that is the VOLUME's multiplier ($k^3$).

practice.q: The radii of two spheres are in the ratio $3:4$. The ratio of their volumes is:
practice.solution: Volumes scale as the cube of the radius ratio: $3^3 : 4^3 = 27 : 64$.
practice.shortcut: $27:64$ (cube the ratio). Trap: $9:16$ — that is the surface-area ratio.

practice.q: A triangular prism has a cross-sectional area of $20$ sq cm and a length of $12$ cm. Its volume is:
practice.shortcut: Area x length. Trap: $120$ (a stray half — prisms carry no $\frac13$ or $\frac12$ factor).

practice.q: A rectangular tank measures $5$ m $\times$ $4$ m $\times$ $3$ m. Its capacity in litres is:
practice.shortcut: $60\ \text{m}^3 \times 1000$ = $60{,}000$ L. Trap: $6{,}000$ (a slipped zero).

practice.q: A pyramid stands on a square base of side $10$ cm and has a height of $12$ cm. Its volume is:
practice.shortcut: One-third of $1200 = 400$. Trap: $1200$ — the containing prism's volume.

practice.q: A pyramid has a rectangular base $12$ cm $\times$ $9$ cm and a height of $10$ cm. Its volume is:
practice.shortcut: $\frac13 \times 1080 = 360$. Trap: $1080$ (no third) — one step, one mark.

practice.q: A bucket is shaped like a frustum of a cone with end radii $5$ cm and $3$ cm and depth $6$ cm. Its capacity is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $\frac{6}{3} = 2$; $2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 49 = 308$. Trap: $264$ — the missing $Rr = 15$ term.

practice.q: A tumbler is a frustum of a cone with radii $4$ cm and $2$ cm and height $21$ cm. Its volume is (take $\pi = 22/7$):
practice.shortcut: $\frac{21}{3} = 7$; $22 \times 28 = 616$. Trap: $440$ (dropping the $Rr = 8$ term).

practice.q: A wooden cube of side $4$ cm is cut into unit cubes (edge $1$ cm). How many small cubes are formed?
practice.shortcut: $4^3 = 64$. Trap: $16$ — that is one FACE of small cubes ($4^2$).

practice.q: Three metallic cubes of edges $3$ cm, $4$ cm and $5$ cm are melted and recast into a single cube. The edge of the new cube is:
practice.shortcut: $\sqrt[3]{216} = 6$ cm. Trap: $12$ cm (the SUM of edges instead of the cube root of the volume sum).

practice.q: A triangular prism has a perimeter of $12$ cm for its cross-section and a length of $10$ cm. Its lateral surface area is:
practice.shortcut: The tube unrolls to $12 \times 10$. Trap: $60$ (a spurious half).

practice.q: A square pyramid has a base edge of $10$ cm and a slant height of $13$ cm. Its lateral surface area is:
practice.solution: Perimeter $= 40$; LSA $= \frac12 P l = \frac12 \times 40 \times 13 = 260$ sq cm.
practice.shortcut: $\frac12 \times 40 \times 13 = 260$. Trap: $520$ (forgot the half) — four triangles, halved each.
